text: Highlife grew up in Ghana (then the Gold Coast) in the early 20th century, blending Akan melodies and rhythms with Western brass bands and guitars. Palm-wine guitar styles and dance bands like E.T. Mensah's, often called the King of Highlife, made it the sound of urban West African nightlife. It later became a root of Afrobeats.

Afrobeats (with an s) took shape in Nigeria and Ghana in the 2000s and 2010s, mixing highlife, hip-hop, dancehall and R&B over bright, syncopated drums. It is different from Fela Kuti's 1970s Afrobeat. Artists such as Wizkid, Burna Boy and Davido carried it to global charts, helped by diaspora scenes in London and beyond.

Afro-fusion is a label artists use for music that blends African rhythms with dancehall, reggae, hip-hop and pop. Burna Boy popularized the term for his own sound. It reflects how diaspora listeners and artists mix the music of home with the music of where they live now.

Amapiano emerged in South Africa's Gauteng townships in the mid-2010s. It grew out of deep house, kwaito and jazz, and is known for its deep, percussive 'log drum' bass and airy piano lines. It spread from local parties and WhatsApp-shared tracks to dance floors worldwide.

Bossa nova was born in Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s, when musicians such as João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim slowed samba down and mixed it with cool jazz harmony. Its hushed vocals and gentle nylon-string guitar, heard in songs like 'The Girl from Ipanema', made it an international sound of calm sophistication.

Reggae developed in Jamaica in the late 1960s out of ska and rocksteady. Its offbeat guitar 'skank' and heavy bass carried messages of resistance, faith and community. Bob Marley and the Wailers made it a global voice, and it shaped dancehall, dub and later hip-hop production.

Lo-fi hip-hop borrows the dusty, sample-based beats of boom-bap producers such as J Dilla and Nujabes and softens them into gentle loops. In the late 2010s, 24/7 YouTube streams turned it into the soundtrack for studying and late-night focus, valued because it sets a mood without demanding attention.

Synthwave appeared in the late 2000s as an homage to 1980s film scores, video games and synth-pop. Kavinsky's 'Nightcall', used in the 2011 film Drive, became a signature track. Its glowing synths evoke night drives and neon cities: nostalgia for a decade many listeners never lived through.

Hip-hop began in the Bronx, New York, in the 1970s. DJ Kool Herc's 1973 parties, where he extended the drum breaks of funk records, are often named as its starting point. Built by Black and Latino youth, it grew into a global culture of rapping, DJing, breaking and graffiti.

Jazz emerged in New Orleans in the early 20th century from African American communities, blending blues, ragtime and brass band traditions. Improvisation is at its heart. It went on to shape almost every form of popular music, from swing and bebop to R&B and hip-hop sampling.

Brian Eno coined 'ambient music' in the 1970s with albums like Music for Airports (1978), describing music that can be listened to closely or ignored. It favors texture and atmosphere over beats and hooks, which is why listeners use it to focus, rest or sleep.

Western classical music spans centuries of composed concert music. Beethoven's 'Moonlight' Sonata (1801), with its slow, rippling first movement, is one of the best-known melancholic piano pieces and is often reimagined by modern producers and film composers.

Country music took shape in the American South in the 1920s from Appalachian folk, blues and gospel. The 1927 Bristol Sessions recordings are often called its 'big bang'. Storytelling about home, work and memory gives it its nostalgic pull.

Folk music is passed down through communities, often by ear. In the 1960s American folk revival, artists such as Joan Baez and Bob Dylan, following Woody Guthrie, used plain acoustic songs to tell stories of hardship and protest. Its intimacy makes it a natural home for sad, reflective songs.

Today's electronic dance music traces back to disco and to Chicago house and Detroit techno in the 1980s, scenes pioneered largely by Black and queer artists in club culture. The 'EDM' label took off in the 2010s festival boom, built around euphoric build-ups and drops.

Heavy metal was forged in Birmingham, England, around 1970, when Black Sabbath slowed down and darkened blues-rock with heavy, distorted guitar riffs. It became a global family of subgenres built on intensity, catharsis and loyal fan communities.

Rock and roll grew out of rhythm and blues, gospel and country in the 1950s United States. Black artists such as Sister Rosetta Tharpe and Chuck Berry pioneered its electric guitar sound long before it became mainstream radio's biggest genre.
Pop is less a single style than the sound of the charts at any moment, built for catchy hooks and wide appeal. It constantly absorbs other genres, from disco and hip-hop to Afrobeats and K-pop.

Indie pop came out of the 1980s UK independent-label scene, where bands on small labels made jangly, melodic, do-it-yourself pop outside the major-label system. 'Indie' still signals music made with fewer gatekeepers.

Rhythm and blues was named in 1949, when Billboard replaced the term 'race records' with it. From 1950s soul to today's smooth, vocal-led R&B, it has been central to Black American music and to how pop expresses romance.

Bedroom pop describes songs recorded at home on laptops and shared on platforms like SoundCloud and Bandcamp, popular from the mid-2010s. Its soft vocals and diary-like lyrics feel private and close, which is why it pairs well with late-night overthinking.
